title: The Sacrifice of the New Creation - 4

content:
Yesterday we studied the fine flour, which speaks of our character. Today we come to the olive oil, which speaks of the Holy Spirit, and then to the wine, which was poured out as a drink offering and speaks of our devotion.

As before, we will ask the practical question of each: how do we actually give this offering to God? Let us begin with the oil.

First, we give ourselves to be saturated, not merely touched. Notice that the oil was mixed into the flour. It was not sprinkled lightly on top. It went all the way through. And this teaches us that the New Creation must let the Spirit of God work into the whole of the character, and not sit only as a surface anointing over a life that has not really changed underneath. It is possible to have a little touch of the Spirit on the outside while the inner life remains dry and untouched. But Yahweh desires that the oil be worked into the flour completely, so that every part of our character is saturated with the Spirit and softened by it. Second, we give ourselves to ongoing filling, not to a single past event. The oil had to be freshly measured for every offering. In the same way, when Paul says, "Be filled with the Holy Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18), he means it as something continual, not a thing that happened once at baptism and need never happen again. We must present ourselves again and again for the Spirit's filling, just as fresh oil was brought each time. Yesterday's filling is not enough for today's need.

Third, we give the oil in increasing measure as our understanding deepens. As with the flour, the oil rose from a fourth of a hin for the lamb, to a third for the ram, to a half for the bull. The lamb-level view of Christ brought a smaller measure; the bull-level view brought a greater one. This means the active presence of the Spirit in our lives should visibly increase as our grasp of Christ's sacrifice increases. The more we understand what Christ has done, the more room we give the Spirit to work, and the more His presence should be seen in the way we live. Fourth, we give room for the oil to produce its specific fruit in season. Oil in Scripture is connected with many things, with joy, with healing, and with the light of understanding. Whatever the Spirit is producing in us at a particular stage of our growth, we must give ourselves over to that work rather than resisting it or limiting it to what is convenient for us. There are seasons when the Spirit works joy in us, seasons when He brings healing, and seasons when He gives fresh light on the Word, and in each season we yield to what He is doing. And fifth, we give ourselves in a way that holds nothing back from the mixture. Oil that stays in the jar does nothing for the flour. It may be present, it may be acknowledged, but if it is never poured into the meal it changes nothing. In the same way, the New Creation must actually let the Spirit be worked into daily decisions, and not merely acknowledge Him with the mind while the daily life goes on unchanged. The oil must leave the jar and enter the flour, or it is of no use at the altar.

Now we come to the wine, the drink offering, which was poured out entirely before Yahweh, and which speaks of our devotion, our very life poured out for Him. Here too there are five ways in which we give it. First, we give it without expecting anything to be returned to us. Unlike the grain offering, from which the priests received a portion to eat, the drink offering had no remainder. It was simply poured out, and nothing came back. And this teaches us that some of our surrender to Yahweh is not for our own benefit or sustenance at all. It is simply poured out for Him. We do not give it in order to receive something back. We give it because He is worthy, and we ask for no return.

Second, we give it as Paul gave it. Paul took the very language of this drink offering and used it to describe his own life. He wrote, "But I will rejoice even if I lose my life, pouring it out like a liquid offering to God" (Philippians 2:17), and again near the end, "As for me, my life has already been poured out as an offering to God" (2 Timothy 4:6). So our surrender is not to be an abstract idea, but a real and personal thing. Each of us, like Paul, must be able to say, "I am now ready to be offered." Third, we give it with joy, and not forcefully. Wine in Scripture is that which gladdens the heart, for the Psalmist says Yahweh gives "wine to make them glad" (Psalm 104:15). So our pouring out should be marked by gladness, not by heavy and reluctant duty. Even as Paul spoke of being poured out, he added, "I want all of you to share that joy" (Philippians 2:17). The poured-out life is a glad life, not a bitter one.

Fourth, we give the wine in increasing measure as our sight of the sacrifice grows. A small view of Christ produces a small and cautious surrender, a devotion carefully measured out to protect ourselves. But a full view of Christ produces a life poured out completely, holding nothing back in reserve. As we see more of what He poured out for us, we pour out more of ourselves in return. And fifth, we give it once and for all in each act, not partially. The wine was poured out; it was not sipped and then saved for later. And every act of surrender must likewise be complete in itself. We are not called to a rationed devotion, carefully measured out to keep back enough of ourselves for safety. We are called to a full pouring at each point of obedience. When Yahweh asks something of us, we pour it out fully, not partly. So as we bring the fine flour of our character, the oil of the Spirit, and the wine of our poured-out devotion, may all three rise together and be full, a whole and pleasing offering to our God, presented through Christ our Lord.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,
Let Your Spirit be worked all the way into our lives, and not rest only upon the surface.

Fill us again and again, for yesterday's filling cannot meet today's need.

Teach us to pour out our lives before You as a drink offering, expecting nothing in return.

Make our surrender glad and not grudging, and complete and not carefully rationed.

Let the flour, the oil, and the wine all rise together, a whole offering unto You.

"My life has already been poured out as an offering to God." - 2 Timothy 4:6

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
